articles.title_orig: Jack Smith, Former Special Counsel Who Charged Trump, Appears Before Congress: Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Jack Smith, Former Special Counsel Who Charged Trump, Appears Before Congress: Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Special counsel Jack Smith, who brought two indictments against now-President Donald Trump in 2023, testified in front of Congress again on Tuesday — this time, to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
Smith’s testimony comes as Republicans continue to probe the investigations into Trump and as some in the party, including the president, have pushed for often-unspecified criminal charges to be brought against Smith.
Here are the major takeaways from Tuesday’s hearing.
Republicans have struggled mightily to substantiate Trump’s desire for Smith to be charged criminally . But rarely has it seemed to backfire like it did Tuesday .
Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri crafted an apparent conspiracy theory about Smith being tied to the prosecution of Trump in Fulton County, Georgia. To substantiate his theory, Schmitt cited text messages he suggested showed Smith had been at an Atlanta Hawks game on February 3, 2024 – the day after Fulton County prosecutor Fani Willis and special prosecutor Nathan Wade admitted to an affair.
Smith appeared dumbfounded, though. He denied going to a Hawks game and said he had no recollection of even being in Atlanta.
“What would you say if I had a series of text messages from your team that said you were in Atlanta at a Warriors-Hawks game on February 3, 2024 – the day after Willis and Wade announced their affair?” Schmitt said.
Schmitt went big on the allegation, telling Smith, “I don’t think you know that we have this stuff.” He urged Smith not to “perjure yourself.” He later called Smith a “dirtbag.” He later told the “Charlie Kirk Show” that he was just asking questions and seeing whether Smith would ensnare himself.
Eventually, Democrats got Schmitt to allow Smith to actually review the evidence – a poster featuring the texts in question. In one of them, a fellow prosecutor asks about a seat being reserved for Smith. The poster showed the Atlanta Hawks’ arena.
But by this point, Smith seemed to put it together. He said he was not at a game featuring the Atlanta Hawks , but rather the University of Iowa Hawkeyes women’s basketball team – which then featured Caitlin Clark – at the University of Maryland in the Washington, DC, area.
Smith’s recollection matches up with a game played that day.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, after clearing up the matter, said Schmitt should apologize.
Schmitt’s office has not responded a request for comment.
At the hearing, he maintained that the texts “could have obviously been related to the prosecution” in Fulton County. He said he stood by calling Smith a “dirtbag.”
The scene epitomized how speculative and thinly constructed the GOP’s allegations about Smith, Trump’s foes and about the justice system being weaponized against Trump have been. Likewise, the GOP’s other major perjury allegation against Smith rests on a complete misreading of the evidence .
But rarely has this apparent fishing expedition been laid so bare. Schmitt seemed to firmly believe he had nailed Smith on something. But just minutes later, it seemed to fall apart – and rather spectacularly so.
Smith is a very careful witness. He often pauses noticeably before answering a question — in a way that can be a little jarring.
But he’s also made clear that he wants to fight back against the Trump administration’s weaponization of the justice system against people like him. And on Tuesday, he was a little more animated and open.
He punctuated his opening statement by saying, “Fear may be contagious; courage is as well.”
He also called it an “outrage” that people he worked with were “targeted illegally, lost their jobs illegally, and had their lives turned upside down by this Department of Justice.”
When asked about the Supreme Court’s 2024 ruling conferring presidents with a large degree of immunity, Smith said it “can be very dangerous for the rule of law” for powerful people to benefit from such exceptions.
He also jousted with lawmakers a little more than he did before, rather than dryly reciting facts.
When GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas asked him whether he had any regrets, Smith said he regretted that “the people I worked with have been unfairly fired and vilified.”
When  Republican Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina claimed Smith unfairly targeted the phone records of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, Smith told her that Lindsey Graham had investigated Trump’s underlying voter-fraud claims and found them to be false.
And he said he won’t be going away quietly.
“I will not be silenced by the continued threats of prosecution from the president or others,” Smith said.
That exchange with Darline Graham was also significant when it comes to learning something new about the attempted prosecutions of Trump.
The reason: Smith said Lindsey Graham was likely to be a witness in the case.
“I believe your brother was a patriotic public servant,” Smith said. “He was not a target of our investigation. In fact, he likely would have been a witness in our case. Your brother investigated the claims that Donald Trump was making. He found them to be false.”
Lindsey Graham publicly broke with Trump on the Senate floor after January 6 (i.e. “ count me out ”) and appeared to be initially helpful to investigators probing the situation.
He later reconciled with Trump and assailed Smith’s investigation when he was among those whose phone records were wrapped up in the probe — and even pushed to get a financial payout for it.
Smith’s comments suggest Graham could have played at least some role in proving the charges against Trump.
The former special counsel seemed to make a point to repeatedly vouch for members of his former staff  who were fired by Trump’s Justice Department and, in some cases, were repeatedly invoked by name at Tuesday’s hearing.
Smith even called them “heroes.”
“My view: These people are heroes, and I believe our country does not recognize and pay enough attention to people like that,” he said. “I think if we did, the partisan things that we’re discussing today – a lot of that would go away.”
Smith also warned about what ousting people like that would portend for the country.
“If you drive those people out of public service, the institutions we rely on for justice, for protecting our country — those institutions are weakened,” Smith said.
When Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff of California talked about how Smith had been attacked, Smith said it was “much more important that the public servants who I work with – that we stop vilifying public servants.”
It’s been nearly a year since Trump appeared alongside then-Attorney General Pam Bondi and claimed Smith had committed crimes.
“Hopefully the Attorney General is looking at what he’s done,” Trump added eight months ago on social media.
There’s been little since then to suggest the Trump administration is able to provide him what he wants. And Tuesday’s hearing often felt like going through the motions more so than anything else.
Apart from Schmitt’s attempt at a gotcha, other Republican lawmakers generally mined territory already covered in the January House Judiciary Committee hearing .
Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri and others repeated an allegation from months ago that Smith perjured himself with his denials about seeking the contents of lawmakers’ communications. But Smith pointed to the holes in that previously debunked theory.
Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana at one point tried to suggest that Smith might have lobbied to become special counsel — the implication being that he had a political agenda and was targeting Trump — but when Smith denied it, Kennedy moved on.
Smith also told lawmakers that he sought to keep secret the phone and other records he was seeking because of concerns that Trump and his allies would try to obstruct justice .

articles.title_zh: China expands overseas military presence with new Laos air force centre
articles.content_orig:
Beijing says jointly operated facilities at Ban Keun Airport will support pilot training and deepen cooperation between the two militaries
China has launched a rare air force support and training centre in Laos, the Ministry of Defence announced on Tuesday.
The China-Laos Joint Support and Training Centre and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy are now in operation at the Ban Keun Airport, aiming to help the Laotian Air Force train its pilots, the ministry said in a statement.
The two institutions will be jointly maintained and operated by both sides, the statement said, without providing details on what personnel or equipment would be based at the airport, or how many personnel or how much equipment.

articles.title_orig: Two Indian nationals charged with smuggling counterfeit Ozempic from China: DOJ
articles.title_zh: Two Indian nationals charged with smuggling counterfeit Ozempic from China: DOJ
articles.content_orig:
Two Indian nationals have been charged in federal court in Florida with an alleged conspiracy to smuggle counterfeit Ozempic from China in a scheme that purportedly continued even after the Food and Drug Administration seized some of the fake weight-loss drugs in 2023 and warned the public about it, the Department of Justice said Tuesday.
One of the men, 33-year-old Swapnadip Roy, was extradited from Italy and made his initial appearance in U.S. District Court in Tampa, Florida, on Tuesday.
Roy and his alleged co-conspirator, Vicky Ramancha, 37, are charged in an indictment with one count of conspiracy to commit smuggling and to defraud the U.S., three counts of smuggling, and two counts of selling counterfeit drugs and holding counterfeit drugs for sale. If convicted, they both face a maximum sentence of 71 years in prison.
Ramancha remains at large.
Court documents state Roy and Ramancha, starting in July 2023 and continuing to the following April, allegedly obtained counterfeit Ozempic from unauthorized sources in China. The popular drug is made by Novo , which recently rebranded from its name Novo Nordisk.
The material they and their co-conspirators allegedly distributed "included counterfeit packaging, package inserts, pen labels, and needles meant to deceive downstream customers into believing they were purchasing authentic Ozempic authorized by the manufacturer," DOJ said.
The case comes as the use of so-called GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic for weight loss has become increasingly popular in the U.S.
In July, Gallup reported that the percentage of U.S. adults who take GLP-1 medications for weight loss purposes rose to 11% in  2026, compared to 3% in 2024.
"And 15% report having used the medicine for weight loss at some point, an increase of nine percentage points" over 2024, Gallup noted.
"Counterfeit prescription drugs — especially common ones — threaten the health and safety of every American who depends on the integrity of our pharmaceutical supply," Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the DOJ's Criminal Division said in a statement Tuesday.
"These defendants allegedly exploited people's health to pay themselves. We will keep pursuing anyone who seeks to deceive American consumers with counterfeit drugs," Duva said.

The Department of Justice has charged a Venezuelan immigrant with assault after he was shot by a federal immigration officer during a traffic stop in Austin, Texas.
Wilber Garcés Pérez, who said he was driving for DoorDash when Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents stopped him on September 20, was sent to a detention center with a bullet still lodged near his spine within hours of the incident, according to his attorney.
An unsealed affidavit signed by a Homeland Security investigator accuses Garcés Pérez of striking an officer in the torso with his car’s side-view mirror before leading agents on what investigators described as a high-speed chase.
The ICE officer, identified only as “L.G.” in the affidavit, was not wearing a body-mounted camera at the time. He shot Garcés Pérez in the back through the back right window of his car. Another officer who was on the scene, identified only as D.F., was wearing a bodycam, but he turned it off during the pursuit.
ICE agents “conducted a law enforcement database” search on Garcés Pérez’s Toyota sedan after noticing it was parked in front of a restaurant with its emergency indicators. The agents “confirmed that a final order of removal had been issued by an immigration judge” against Garcés Pérez, who was registered with the car, according to the affidavit.
After Garcés Pérez returned to his car and started driving, D.F. “activated his emergency lights” but Garcés Pérez “did not pull over and stop his car immediately,” according to the document.
Garcés Pérez pulled over to the shoulder of the road, and L.G.’s unmarked ICE SUV parked diagonally in front of him.
L.G. then approached the driver’s side door near the sideview mirror and D.F. stood beside him.
Garcés Pérez “rolled down his window slightly” as they spoke, and he provided his driver’s license, the filing says. After the officers asked him to step out of the car, Garcés Pérez “ignored the request” and “engaged in a Spanish conversation with L.G. about moving the car and parking it,” the document says.
“The conversational tone was pleasant and not aggressive,” according to the affidavit.
One minute later, Garcés Pérez “abruptly closed the window and drove off,” the filing states.
Officer L.G. “tried to avoid contact with the car” but the “driver’s side-view mirror struck L.G. in his torso as it drove off,” according to the Justice Department.
Garcés Pérez has said that he asked to move his car so that his wife could collect it.
He told reporters last week that he initially believed an unmarked SUV was trying to hit his car, and he continued along his delivery route to avoid what he thought was an aggressive driver.
The SUV then hit his car and turned its police lights on, he said. Officers then blocked him from moving his car to the shoulder of the road, but Garcés Pérez tried to make a loop to park the car in a secure spot, he said.
The affidavit claims Garcés Pérez then led the officers on a “high-speed chase through a commercial and residential area.”
Officers turned on their lights and sirens, and D.F. “lost sight” of L.G. and Garcés Pérez while he was calling for assistance from a dispatcher, according to the document.
“D.F. at that point turned off his body-worn camera,” the filing says.
D.F. tried to call L.G., who didn’t answer. L.G. then called him back and claimed Garcés Pérez “attempted to strike L.G. with his car and L.G. had fired his pistol,” the affidavit says.
Garcés Pérez was initially sent to a hospital. But four hours later, with a bullet still lodged near his spine, Garcés Pérez was moved to the South Texas ICE Processing Center, where he writhed in pain without a bed or medication, according to his lawyer.
He was moved to another hospital after complaining of paralysis.
His legal team has filed a lawsuit seeking his release from custody and to block his removal from the country. A judge has set a hearing for September 30, according to court records.
The incident is the latest in a streak of shootings by ICE agents during traffic stops in recent months, including the killings of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who were fatally shot within days of each other in July.
Donald Trump’s administration has sought to characterize the shootings as justified before any investigations were performed, let alone completed, while video evidence and witness statements either contradicted official narratives or raised critical questions about the use of lethal force.
Homeland Security said Garcés Pérez is in “stable” condition and remains in federal custody pending his removal from the U.S.
The agency claims Garcés Pérez illegally entered the U.S. during Joe Biden’s administration, but his attorney said he legally entered using the CBP One app, which allowed noncitizens to schedule appointments at ports of entry to seek legal entry and seek asylum and other immigration relief before arriving at the U.S. border.
Last year, the Trump administration abruptly ended the program and moved to terminate legal status for every person who used the app to enter the country, leaving tens of thousands of immigrants vulnerable to arrest and removal.
In March, a federal judge determined that those blanket cancellations were unlawful.
“His immigration matters do not negate his humanity. At all,” his attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch said last week. “This man belongs at home in Austin with his wife.”

articles.content_orig:
Coinbase Ventures and CMCC Global closed a strategic funding round with Raven, a trading firm, at a $90 million pre-money valuation.
Founded in 2023, Raven provides liquidity in crypto trading but has expanded into prediction markets since the second quarter of 2025, according to cofounder, Petar Kostov.
" Venues without enough trading volume often struggle to find a liquidity partner at all. Venues with a lot of trading volume often struggle to find enough liquidity to keep up," Kostov told CNBC.
Coinbase Ventures and CMCC Global confirmed the funding round with CNBC. Coinbase Ventures is the investment arm of Crypto platform Coinbase , which introduced prediction markets in its trading app last December. CMCC Global is a Hong Kong-based investor focused on blockchain technology.
"We are excited to support Raven's next phase of growth as they expand the business and continue to dominate liquidity on the venues that they serve," said Charlie Morris, CMCC co-founder. Morris has joined Raven's board of directors and will work with management to expand among institutions.
Raven serves as an institutional market-maker for prediction markets, generating constant buy and sell orders on contracts, giving traders liquidity to enter and exit positions. But the company wears multiple hats, Kostov said.
"Early on, we advise on the technical setup and on market design, from API specifications to which markets to list first. At launch, we provide the opening liquidity. After launch, we stay in the book and help the venue expand into new categories as it grows," he added.
The firm provides liquidity on prediction market platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket, while also participating in both non-U.S. regulated or on-chain venues, according to Raven's website. Raven has quoted more than 3,000 contracts, including sports, crypto, macroeconomics and entertainment.
Raven was an established high-frequency trading firm providing liquidity across centralized and decentralized exchanges before entering prediction markets.
According to The Block, the company raised $2.7 million in a seed funding round at a $25 million valuation, with Hack VC leading. Wintermute Ventures with other angel investors were also in a 2024 round.
Raven declined to comment on how much Coinbase and CMCC each invested in the latest round.

articles.title_orig: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer now questions whether she killed her 3 children
articles.title_zh: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer now questions whether she killed her 3 children
articles.content_orig:
Defendant Lindsay Clancy looks at the jury after Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial in Clancy's murder trial on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger via AP hide caption
Lindsay Clancy's lawyer argued Tuesday that there wasn't enough evidence to prove she killed her three children, a striking turn after a lengthy trial that focused more on her mental state than on whether she took their lives.
"This entire case is based on speculation," attorney Kevin Reddington said during the first hearing since Clancy's trial ended Sept. 4 with a deadlocked jury. They were split 11 to 1 in her favor.
During that trial, Reddington didn't dispute that Clancy killed the children at the family's home in 2023. Instead, the defense sought to persuade the jury that the 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse was not criminally responsible because of mental disease, a rare condition called postpartum psychosis. ___
EDITOR'S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. ___
But at Tuesday's hearing, Reddington sought to persuade Judge William Sullivan — the same judge who presided over the first trial — to acquit Clancy.
There is, Reddington contended, not enough evidence "that this woman killed those children." He pointed to matters ranging from her condition when she was found, badly injured and bleeding in the yard outside her home, to her lack of memory of what happened when she woke up in a hospital. At the first trial, her now ex-husband and first responders testified that they arrived at the house and discovered she had tried to kill herself right after killing the children.
"Where is the admission? Where does she say that she did this?" Reddington asked, going on to recap his arguments that she also was psychotic and delusional at the time of the children's deaths. He didn't offer any alternative theories or evidence about who might be responsible.
Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham called his argument "laughable," pointing to various evidence raised during the trial. In court papers filed Monday, prosecutors recapped their arguments that there was enough evidence to convict Clancy.
The prosecution maintains that Clancy knew her actions were wrong when she used exercise bands to strangle 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan Clancy. They said she contrived to get her husband out of the house that evening by sending him to pick up medicine for one of their children and dinner for the family.
The judge didn't immediately decide, and no trial date was set.
Prosecutors have yet to decide whether to retry Clancy, Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said after the hearing. They could choose to retry her on first-degree murder charges or seek to try her only on lesser charges, including second-degree murder or manslaughter, or drop the case entirely.
"We are going to do what we can for the children," Cruz told reporters outside the court. "That is what this case is about."
Clancy's attorneys have also asked the judge to dismiss the criminal case. Among other things, they have argued that the judge should have ousted the one juror who favored a murder conviction after the jury foreperson complained he was refusing to listen to the law on reasonable doubt.
The juror, Michael Desronvil, has said through his lawyer that he had no doubts about his stance. Desronvil told Fox News' "Hannity" in a brief video statement on Monday that "the whole focus has been on me, but we want to reel everything back and put the focus on the three angels," meaning the children.
The livestreamed trial generated intense public interest and drew attention to maternal mental health after childbirth. About a dozen Clancy supporters, most dressed in pink, stood outside court Tuesday waiting for her to arrive.
Clancy remains charged with murder and is expected to stay at a psychiatric hospital until her case is resolved.
Clancy could have been sentenced to life in prison if convicted of murder. If acquitted, the judge could have ordered her confined to a mental health facility.

articles.title_orig: New York Times executive fatally shot by elderly in-laws, police say
articles.title_zh: New York Times executive fatally shot by elderly in-laws, police say
articles.content_orig:
A New York Times executive was fatally shot in California, allegedly by his wife's elderly parents who have been arrested on suspicion of murder.
Jonathan McKinsey, 40, the newspaper's director of engineering for games player experience, was found with multiple gunshot wounds in a car park in Dublin - 35 miles (56km) east of San Francisco - on Saturday afternoon, police said.
Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, his parents-in-law who are both 77 years old, are facing multiple charges, including first-degree murder.
It was unclear whether the couple have a lawyer, and they are due to appear in court to formally face the charges on Wednesday.
McKinsey's death was confirmed by the New York Times, which produces several games and puzzles, including popular word game Wordle.
His body was found at 15:00 (22:00 GMT) on Thursday afternoon outside the Dublin Sports Grounds.
Witnesses told KGO-TV in San Francisco that they heard a flurry of gunshots, before seeing the victim on the ground.
"I saw the guy drop to the floor: head bloody and chest bloody," witness Assad Razawi told the news outlet.
His daughter added that her father saw the couple "walking together and then casually walk away from the shooting".
The couple were arrested several minutes later by an officer passing by the scene. They had remained in the area after the attack, a witness said.
Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen were arrested at the scene
McKinsey was pronounced dead at the scene, according to police.
Police have not disclosed any motive for his killing.
The elderly couple are being held at the Santa Rita jail.
They also face charges of felony conspiracy, wilful discharge of a firearm with gross negligence, and child endangerment.
McKinsey, who is transgender, and his wife had been involved in several legal disputes this past year, and they filed for divorce in December.
They were still engaged in a child-custody battle when he was killed, and each had filed for domestic abuse restraining orders against the other.
According to the New York Times, he had accused his in-laws of abusing him because of his gender identity.
Last year, McKinsey pleaded guilty to two misdemeanour charges of domestic abuse after he was accused of slapping one child, and leaving another child at home while he was shopping.

Flash flooding and winds meteorologists described as "life-threatening" accompanied Hurricane Polo as it made landfall early Tuesday in Baja California, Mexico.
According to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami , the Category 2 storm hit land slightly south of Las Barrancas. Roughly 80 miles (130 kilometers) north of Cabo San Lazaro and 70 miles (115 kilometers) south of Mulege, the system carried maximum sustained winds of 110 mph (175 kph) and moved northeast at 13 mph (20 kph).
Officials noted that Polo had previously reached Category 3 status on Monday, recording peak winds of 115 mph (185 kph). Rainfall totals of 6-12 inches (about 15 to 30 centimeters) were projected to soak regions across Baja California Sur.
Heavy rain and severe flooding could also extend into portions of the U.S. Southwest as the week progresses, following earlier forecasts warning of dangerous winds and intense flash floods as Polo moved toward mainland Mexico.
Concurrently, Tropical Storm Rachel was tracking parallel to the Mexican coastline early Tuesday morning. About 300 miles (485 kilometers) west-southwest of Acapulco and 315 miles (505 kilometers) south of Manzanillo, Rachel had sustained winds of 60 mph (95 kph) as it moved west-northwest at 12 mph (19 kph).
Elsewhere in the Pacific , Hurricane Nolo remained a major storm on Monday evening, though it was gradually moving away from Hawaii .
Baja California peninsula was preparing for Polo
In the northern Mexican state of Sonora , officials announced Monday night the suspension of all "nonessential" public operations, halting academic, athletic, and non-critical work functions across the capital and over a dozen surrounding municipalities.
Naval forces in Mexico mobilized personnel along the northern Pacific shore, dispatching three ships equipped to deliver emergency supplies to seaside towns stranded by the weather. Local leaders on the Baja California Peninsula opened temporary shelters, while regional ports were shut down and local travel was halted.
Pacific storm activity greater than normal this season
Tropical weather in the Pacific basin has outpaced typical levels at the height of the season, National Weather Service lead forecaster Bob Oravec noted. He pointed out that this elevated activity aligns with El Niño cycles, which often produce more tropical systems.
Downpours are anticipated to spread across the U.S. Southwest, dropping several inches of rain over Texas , New Mexico , Utah , and Arizona . The region's dry terrain and sparse plant cover leave rocky canyons particularly vulnerable to sudden inundation, Andrew Mangham, senior service hydrologist for the National Weather Service based in Albuquerque , New Mexico, explained.
"We’re getting caught up here in a very, very short time," Mangham said. "And that’s not really what we want. We want nice rains, you know, all summer long."
Floods and mudslides remain a risk in Hawaii
By Monday, Hurricane Nolo was located roughly 425 miles (685 kilometers) west-southwest of Honolulu and 330 miles (535 kilometers) south-southeast of French Frigate Shoals. The storm maintained top winds of 120 mph (195 kph) while advancing north-northwest at 15 mph (24 kph).
Over the weekend, Nolo brought heavy rainfall to southern and southeastern areas of Hawaii's Big Island . A Facebook update from the U.S. National Guard confirmed that Hawaii National Guard personnel pulled 19 residents to safety from floodwaters over the weekend.
As the system moved toward the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument, a protected marine reserve, weather forecasters cautioned that hazardous conditions could affect the area beginning Tuesday.

British counterterrorism police are leading an investigation after five men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offenses and preparing a terrorist act near an air base used by U.S. forces.
Police received a report at around 12:45 a.m. Sunday about three suspicious vehicles traveling toward RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwestern England. Armed officers responded and arrested the men in nearby Whelford.
Fairford is used as a forward operating location for the U.S. Air Force Global Strike Command. The base has hosted U.S. B-52 and B-1 bombers during the Iran war , according to ABC News . American forces have used Fairford to carry out strikes against Iranian missile sites, the Associated Press reported.
Read More: Why More Republicans Are Breaking With Trump on Iran
In a press conference Sunday, Assistant Chief Constable Richard Ocone said that about 85 households in the area were advised to evacuate early Sunday morning as a precaution.
"A 400m cordon has been put in place around the vehicles, while the Army's Explosive Ordnance Disposal Unit examine them,” Ocone said. A statement from police earlier Sunday said that they believe the situation is “contained.”
Aerial footage from Sky News shows a bomb disposal robot moving between three white vans at the site, with the rear doors of two vehicles open.
Ocone added that the men remain in custody and will be questioned by police.
The base is home to both the 501st Combat Support Wing Headquarters and the 420th Air Base Squadron, and serves as the “preferred bomber forward operating location in Europe,” according to the U.S. Air Force.
TIME has reached out to the U.S. Air Force for comment on the incident.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who assumed the post in July, called the incident “deeply concerning” on X .
“The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe,” he wrote. “The investigation remains ongoing, and I would urge people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts.” When asked by reporters about the arrests, U.S. President Donald Trump called them “fantastic.” “They were looking to do big damage to our fort,” Trump said of the suspects, “and working with the British worked out great.”
Trump also said the suspects had been under surveillance before their arrests. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” he said.
British police have not confirmed that RAF Fairford was the intended target of the suspected attacks. The Associated Press reported that investigators were considering a possible connection to Iran, but no such link has been confirmed.

articles.title_zh: Potential Taiwan tension sparked ‘last minute’ change in Trump-Xi National Archives visit
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump (2nd-L) speaks to Archivist of the United States Bradford Wilson (L) as he views the U.S. Constitution during a tour of the National Archives Museum alongside first lady Melania Trump, President of China Xi Jinping and first lady of China Peng Liyuan on September 25, 2026 in Washington, DC. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images hide caption
On Friday, the National Archives Museum prepared to welcome President Trump and the Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Inside the museum's main foyer, a long table had been set up in the center of the room that morning, with a temporary display resting on the black tablecloth showcasing a brick from the Great Wall of China and an elaborate 19th century scroll sent by a Qing emperor.
But the entire display was removed, due to a "last minute" change in the event, according to a Chinese diplomat granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
The sudden change was precipitated because of Chinese displeasure over one document that the U.S. had planned to show: the Treaty of San Francisco of 1951, according to the diplomat and two other people familiar with the matter granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
Beijing was irate over the Treaty of San Francisco "because the U.S. and Japan signed it, but not China," according to one of the Chinese diplomats.
The treaty, which ended World War II hostilities between Japan and the Allied Powers, including the U.S. Both Trump and Xi referenced last week how the two countries fought together on the same side during the conflict. But the treaty also leaves the status of Taiwan undetermined and does not state that the island belongs to Beijing.
"It is a point of contention for the Chinese because they were not signatories to the Treaty of San Francisco, and they do not like the fact that the treaty of SF leaves undetermined Taiwan's political status," said Ryan Hass , a Taiwan and China expert at the think tank Brookings Institution in Washington.
An administration official speaking on anonymity because they are not authorized to speak on the record told NPR the group at the archives viewed "important, historic documents that set the foundation for 250 years of American greatness."
"The visit offered an opportunity for both leaders to discuss the United States and China's history and concluded a very productive state visit between the two leaders," the official said.
The Chinese embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.
Other documents key to defining the U.S.' relationship to Taiwan were also discussed for possible display, according to U.S. officials involved in the visit planning, namely the Six Assurances and the Three Communiques , but those documents were ultimately not included.
The incident shows how sensitive Taiwan remains in the U.S.-China relationship and how minute differences in historical interpretation continue to have foreign policy consequences.
The discussion to include Taiwan-related documents, which would almost certainly anger Beijing, are also an indication of pushback from within the U.S. government against President Trump's warm reception of Xi, and sparked in part by concerns that Xi would try to change the U.S.' official stance towards Taiwan.
Taiwan, a democratic island which China hopes to control one day, has its own government and military, but Beijing is opposed to the island declaring formal independence. The U.S. does not have formal relations with Taiwan nor does it have any commitment to defend Taiwan should China ever attack the island. However, through a web of American legislation and diplomatic statements, including the Six Assurances and Three Communiques, the U.S. remains the island's main security guarantor.
"I think the trip to the National Archives was intended to reciprocate Xi Jinping's hospitality in Beijing when he took Donald Trump to the Temple of Heaven and the private tour of the gardens in Zhongnanhai [the central leadership compound in Beijing]. And the symbolism of Xi Jinping showing the Temple of Heaven and what that stood for and President Trump showing America's foundational documents and how they inform America's approach to China, I think it sends a signal of the parameters of limits in which President Trump operates," said Hass.
The Chinese embassy found out about the list of documents shown on Thursday, during Xi's state visit to Washington, according to two Chinese diplomats.
Ninety minutes before the two leaders arrived at the National Archives, Chinese diplomats said it was unclear if the Treaty of San Francisco would be on display.
The Treaty of San Francisco explicitly leaves Taiwan's sovereign status as undetermined, and Taiwanese leaders often cite the treaty to argue that Taiwan should have the right to self-determination over its sovereignty.
Beijing has intensified its criticism of the Treaty of San Francisco since late last year, which it does not recognize , and in private, has requested other countries to consider the document illegal, according to U.S. diplomats, because neither the governments of China nor Taiwan signed it.
On Taiwan, China prefers instead to reference the Cairo Declaration and Potsdam Declaration in which U.S. leaders supported the cessation of Japanese territories, and "restore" them to Chinese sovereignty under the "Republic of China," though that moniker now refers to the government which presides over Taiwan.
When President Trump and Chinese leader Xi walked up red-carpeted stairs into the Archives in Washington D.C., the building's foyer had been cleared, and the two men browsed original copies of the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution, and the Bill of Rights.
Xi praised the "founding spirit" of 250 years of U.S. history in the archives. "Ours goes 250 years, which is great," Trump said, "and we're proud of it, but theirs goes 6,000 years."

"His own words and that of his staff have told the tale of rampant wrongdoing and political conduct," he said.
Grassley said his investigation will continue.
When asked by GOP Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina if he wishes he did anything differently during his time as special counsel, Smith said that his limited public statements allowed others to misrepresent his investigations without a public rebuttal.
Smith said he began his career operating under the presumption that "you only do your talking in the courtroom, and that you don't talk on the courthouse steps." But, he added, "if you stick to that and that alone, people can unfairly malign your team, and unfairly malign you and your case in a way, and you really can't respond."
"You don't want to interfere with someone's right to a fair trial, and you don't want to get down in the gutter and start calling people names. But at the same time, there are things being put out daily that are patently untrue, and you know they're untrue," Smith said.
"I'm not advocating that prosecutors in the future start going on the internet every day responding to comments, but I do think that the school of prosecution I came from, where you only speak in the courtroom — I do agree that prosecutors in the future need to learn to be able to communicate to the outside world, because I believe strongly we did our investigation the right way, but I limited myself in who I talked to about that," Smith said, pointing to the two short announcements he did in his time as special counsel.
Sen. Ted Cruz, a Republican from Texas, questioned Smith about nondisclosure orders issued by a court that prevented phone carriers from disclosing that they had received subpoenas for toll records from senators' phones.
When asked why he sought the nondisclosure orders, Smith said his team had "strong reason to believe that Donald Trump would destroy evidence."
"We do not have to wait for someone to be injured for an investigation to be obstructed," he said. "We had strong reason to believe that Donald Trump would obstruct our investigation, given the obstruction alleged in the Florida indictment, given the attempts to intimidate witnesses in the election case, given the threats that were later made to witnesses in the election case."
Prosecutors alleged in the indictment in the classified documents case that the president attempted to obstruct the FBI and grand jury probe and hide documents. They said the president directed an aide, Walt Nauta, to move boxes of records to hide them from a lawyer and the FBI, and suggested his lawyer should hide or destroy documents sought by a grand jury subpoena.
Smith's team also said in court papers that the president attempted to delete security camera footage at Mar-a-Lago to hide information from the FBI.
In the elections case, Smith wrote in his final report that Mr. Trump made threatening public statements targeting likely witnesses and resorted to intimidation.
"Disclosure of that subpoena could result in Donald Trump attempting to intimidate witnesses as he had before and after," the former special counsel said.
Smith said his office sought to follow Justice Department policy and federal law when pursuing the nondisclosure orders.
"We submitted these nondisclosure orders consistent with the law and department policy," he said.
When asked whether he had any regrets about his work as special counsel, Smith said he did.
"I regret that the people I worked with have been unfairly fired and vilified," he said.
Sen. Darlene Graham, who replaced her brother Sen. Lindsey Graham in the Senate after his death, alleged that Smith accused him of potentially attempting to destroy evidence, intimidate witnesses or cause harm to his investigation. Smith pushed back, saying that Lindsey Graham "likely" would have been a witness if the 2020 election case had gone to trial.
Lindsey Graham, a four-term senator who was seeking reelection, died suddenly in July, and Darlene Graham, his younger sister, was appointed to the seat. She won a special primary in August to replace him on the ballot in November.
"I believe your brother was a patriotic public servant. He was not a target of our investigation, and in fact, he likely would have been a witness in our case," Smith said. "Your brother investigated the claims that Donald Trump was making. He found them to be false."
Last year, GOP senators said that the FBI analyzed phone records of more than half a dozen Republican lawmakers, including Lindsey Graham, during Smith's investigation. Smith has repeatedly said Tuesday that he only got toll records showing the duration of the senators phone calls and who they were talking to, and not the contents of the calls themselves.
Darlene Graham responded that she believes Smith was "just trying to bully my brother and other allies of President Trump."
"You caused my brother and a lot of other senators a lot of stress, and that makes me sick," Graham continued. "You should be ashamed of yourself. It's also a damn shame that you weaponized our legal system to do this. To go after a political opponent and his allies, including Lindsey, what a disgrace to our justice system and the Constitution that you would stoop this low. Shame on you!"
Smith was pressed by Sen. Eric Schmitt, a Republican from Missouri, about whether he attended a NBA game between the Atlanta Hawks and Golden State Warriors in Atlanta in early February 2024.
Schmitt said Smith's alleged attendance at the game would be significant because the game occurred around the time that Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis revealed she had a romantic relationship with Nathan Wade, whom she hired as a special prosecutor to work on an investigation into alleged efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 election in Georgia.
Smith said he did not attend that game, but may have flown through Atlanta on the way to Florida. Still, he told senators he "definitely did not go" to an Atlanta Hawks game.
The former special counsel also said he never met Wade or Willis while he was special counsel.
Schmitt then displayed a poster board with text messages from members of Smith's team, including one asking if "109 Row 1" was reserved for Smith. Schmitt said the messages showed Smith was in Atlanta and attended the NBA game on Feb. 3, 2024.
"I don't think you know that we have this stuff, so I'll give you a second to process it so you don't, you know, perjure yourself," Schmitt told Smith.
But the poster board on display was quickly taken down by Schmitt's staff and Smith asked to see it again.
Schmitt said he would put the information "in a follow-up."
"I think you've already perjured yourself," the senator said, calling Smith a "total dirtbag."

Texts, including unnamed male defendant appearing to apologize, reportedly sent days after alleged 2024 assault
Excerpts of text messages reportedly exchanged by a defendant in the Cornell University gang-rape case and the woman who claims she was assaulted were published by CBS News on Tuesday, a day after New York prosecutors said they were reopening a criminal investigation.
The texts were reportedly sent within days of the alleged October 2024 assault at a campus fraternity house in which a female student said she was drugged and repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours by multiple men who were alerted to her presence on the social media platform Snapchat.
Taken together, the texts seem to highlight the complications that have often presented themselves in investigations centering on rape on college campuses in the US.
In one of the messages, screenshots of which were obtained by CBS New York , the unnamed male defendant appears to apologize to the woman for “how things went down” – and said his memory of events two nights previously was “kinda fuzzy”.
He said he and another male who was present regretted that they were too intoxicated to “shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand”.
In reply, the woman, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, and has since left Cornell, said her memory was “super clouded too” and that they were all intoxicated.
According to CBS, she also wrote: “non[e] of the sexual stuff was illegal”, and stated that she liked being with him and another man. Later, she suggested they smoke together again, “but like leave out the extra 5 billion men and ketamine”.
A civil lawsuit filed by the woman earlier in September alleges that seven men, named as Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar, assaulted her at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house after she went there in an intoxicated state looking for a friend.
Two of the alleged perpetrators were subsequently expelled after an internal investigation by Cornell – while the other five were allowed to resume their studies at the Ivy League institution after writing an essay, attending a workshop, or serving a short suspension.
None was ever arrested or charged, and outrage over the treatment of the alleged offenders grew when the woman’s lawsuit was made public.
On Monday, the Tompkins county, New York , district attorney Matthew Van Houten – whose office’s jurisdiction includes Cornell – said he had reopened the dormant investigation into the case. He said his office did that in light of allegations that he said were “dramatically different” from those originally made by the alleged victim.
He also issued a statement defending his initial decision not to seek charges.
“Jane Doe’s sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped,” Van Houten said.
“On the contrary, [her] statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual. My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later.”
CBS, meanwhile, also claimed to have a video of Snapchat messages exchanged on the night of the alleged assault by numerous members of a group called Chi Phi Actives. One of the messages, sent while the woman was in the since-closed fraternity house, allegedly stated there was “free pussy upstairs”.
According to CBS, a later message sent by a group member asked: “Shop still open?” The response was, “Yea”.
Attorney Thomas Giuffra, who represents the woman, confirmed to CBS that his client – named Jane Doe in court documents – exchanged text messages with one defendant after the alleged assault. But Giuffra said he could not be certain the screenshots that CBS News saw were authentic.
Giuffra, according to CBS, said Doe was in denial and traumatized afterwards, had been intoxicated to the point of incapacity that night, and was trying to find out what happened.
He said she felt as if she would not take an aggressive tone with this particular defendant if she wanted answers.
Further details released on Monday by Van Houten included a summary of a “six-page, single-spaced, typewritten statement” that the woman gave Cornell University police after she reported the assault three weeks after it was alleged to have taken place.
In it, she admits she was initially willing to have sex with two of the Chi Phi members – before the others showed up and joined in. She said she was plied with alcohol, marijuana and ketamine, was “slapped” multiple times, and said her “phone was on the other side of the room and she felt as if there was no way for her to escape this room full of predatory, fraternity men”.
Two of the defendants, Kretzschmar and Norris, denied their involvement in statements to ABC News , either directly or through lawyers.
TMZ reported on Tuesday that a third defendant, Sarabia, had been fired from his job with Wells Fargo. The bank did not return a request for comment.

A massive roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain has closed permanently after passengers allegedly suffered a series of catastrophic brain injuries .
The Valencia theme park’s president Brian Oerding announced on Tuesday that after almost 20 years of the X2 in operation, the park made the decision to permanently retire the roller coaster.
“While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it’s the right thing to do,” Oerding wrote in a theme park blog post.
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
“Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously.”
The X2 initially opened in 2002 as the X roller coaster before undergoing upgrades and reopening as X2 in 2008, KTLA reported .
It was the world’s first fourth-dimensional roller coaster, reaching speeds of nearly 80 mph, with seats that could rotate 360 degrees during drops of up to 200 feet.
Oerding ended his post about how the ride “has welcomed more than 16 million guests and earned a passionate following among ride enthusiasts.”
“We recognize the special place X2 holds in the coaster community, and we are grateful to our team members who operated and maintained it throughout its run.”
The closure comes on the heels of two deaths and a dozen injuries linked to the thrill ride at the park over the past 24 years.
The coaster has been shut down since July 12 after two riders suffered catastrophic injuries and needed emergency brain surgery in incidents just days apart this summer, according to an investigation by CNN .
Earlier this month, three new lawsuits were filed against the park, and a manufacturer of the X2 coaster, from people who alleged the coaster caused them traumatic brain injury, ABC7 News reported.
One of those involved in the suit is a 25-year-old woman, who is still on a ventilator months after she allegedly suffered a catastrophic brain injury on the ride.
Naomi Greer-Wilkinson is seen in photos surrounded by medical equipment, a breathing tube running from a tracheostomy in her neck, while another image shows her wearing a cervical collar.
Doctors who treated Greer-Wilkinson and another woman injured on the ride told CNN the brain injuries were the result of a “traumatic rapid acceleration-deceleration event” experienced while riding X2.
Greer-Wilkinson was injured just six days after Pamela Guillen suffered a similar medical emergency on the same coaster while celebrating her daughter Camille Marquez’s 16th birthday.
Attorneys representing injured riders say more than 100 people have come forward in recent months claiming they suffered some form of brain injury after riding the roller coaster, the DailyMail reported .
“These people went to Magic Mountain for some entertainment, or some family fun, and they suffered catastrophic brain damage,” said attorney Gary Dordick, with the firm that filed the three new lawsuits, NBC Los Angeles reported.
Guillen ultimately regained consciousness and has been undergoing rehabilitation, while Greer-Wilkinson remains hospitalized.
In June 2022, 22-year-old Christopher Hawley collapsed and lost consciousness shortly after riding X2 with his brother and cousin.
He died from a traumatic brain injury the following day, with a surgeon describing damage akin to shaken baby syndrome in the skull of the San Diego State University graduate.
Hawley’s death was ruled an accident caused by blunt head trauma from a park ride by the Los Angeles County medical examiner.
His family sued Six Flags in 2023. In August, his parents reached an undisclosed settlement with Magic Mountain and the supplier of X2’s replacement trains.

articles.title_zh: Trump touts America.gov, but its government-sourced AI answers undercut many of his statements
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he signed a "morally binding" AI document with tech leaders following a highly anticipated luncheon at White House , as calls for a slowdown reach a fever pitch.
Flanked by major tech leaders, Trump talked up the benefits of data centers and pushed for artificial intelligence self-regulation.
"There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation, and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that," Trump told reporters after the event. "But the self-regulation is very important."
Trump called data centers a "very positive thing" despite mounting backlash over the sprawling multibillion-dollar facilities ahead of the midterm elections. He also told reporters that he officially changed AI to "super intelligence."
Tech leaders "want to see communities that are safe and happy, and they're going to make communities very, very happy," he said. "Otherwise, they'll be forced to go overseas or other locations."
Outside the White House, Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su said she was "very encouraged" by Tuesday's event and there was "a lot of optimism and a sense of responsibility" in the room. Leaders also discussed some specifics for a framework and industry accountability, she said.
"I mean, at the end of the day, it's our responsibility to show the power of the technology as well as ensure that it's very safe," Su told reporters.
Concerns over the rapid pace of AI development have intensified in Washington and Silicon Valley as cases of agent-orchestrated attacks mount and major researchers warn of serious consequences for humanity.
Frontier lab leaders Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman have joined the calls for a slowdown, facing off against leading tech peers and the president, who previously blasted AI safety fears as a "hoax" and a "scam."
Trump said executives want to "do the right thing" for the U.S. following Tuesday's meeting.
This week, OpenAI postponed the release of its latest GPT-6.1 Astra model over safety concerns. Just last week, the company said it was conducting an "extensive" review of model behavior.
The AI lab has disclosed several incidents of unauthorized model behavior since the infamous Hugging Face attack sparked concerns over rogue AI earlier this summer.
A luncheon seating chart posted to Trump's Truth Social account on Tuesday showed the president seated next to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , followed by Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and Google 's Sundar Pichai.
Opposite the president sat Vice President JD Vance, between Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Johnson.
Other attendees included Microsoft 's Satya Nadella, Anthropic 's Dario Amodei and Tom Brown, OpenAI 's president Greg Brockman and senior administration officials such as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
OpenAI is simultaneously hosting its annual DevDay developer conference in San Francisco. John Ternus, Apple 's new CEO, did not appear on the list.
"The main issue that you have and I have is we have to take responsibility for the dangers we're aware of," Palantir CEO Alex Karp told CNBC outside the White House on Tuesday ahead of the event. "All of us do. And by the way, American people don't want separate rules for tech people and for themselves."
The luncheon coincided with an all-day event hosted by the president and vice president, where the administration unveiled a new AI-powered chatbot for government websites.
Ahead of Tuesday's White House lunch, Anthropic's Amodei attended a private dinner Sunday with the president , following his striking absence from a state dinner for the Chinese president. Sunday's dinner was the first one-on-one gathering between the two leaders, according to a person familiar with the visit.
Trump has long maintained that the U.S. needs to maintain its competitive edge on AI.
"These are the most brilliant people in the world, and the job they've done is unbelievable," Trump said on Tuesday. "We have a very big lead, and we're going to keep our lead, and it's a very positive thing."

articles.title_orig: What to know about Christa Pike, first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years
articles.title_zh: What to know about Christa Pike, first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years
articles.content_orig:
Tennessee is set to execute Christa Pike , the only woman on its death row, by lethal injection on Wednesday. If the procedure happens as scheduled, Pike would also become the only woman executed in the state in the last 200 years.
Now 50, Pike has been incarcerated since 1995 for the murder that year of her former classmate, Colleen Slemmer. According to court records, Pike and Slemmer were students at the Job Corps Center in Knoxville when Pike, then 18, tortured and killed her, allegedly over comments Slemmer, 19, had made about her relationship.
Pike's boyfriend and another friend helped carry out the attack and murder, the records said.
Pike's case has drawn international attention and some outcry, with the United Nations recently joining local advocacy groups in their calls for Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence .
Their criticisms mainly center on the childhood abuse and untreated mental illness from which Pike suffered when Slemmer was killed, factors that play much larger roles in how juries make sentencing decisions now than they did at Pike's trial. U.N. experts also said the decades Pike spent in isolation on death row, as the sole woman awaiting execution in Tennessee, should amount to unlawful torture.
But Lee announced on Monday that he was denying Pike's clemency petition, allowing her execution to move forward. In a statement, her attorneys said they were "deeply saddened and heartbroken" by the announcement and noted how much their client had changed while incarcerated.
"The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists," the statement said. "Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper treatment for her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women."
One of her attorneys, Luke Ihnen, told CBS News that "in her classic Christa way, she has spent her last days worried more about her friends, family and legal team than herself."
In a statement included with her clemency petition , Pike said she recognized that the ramifications of her crime have been "huge, unforgettable and ruined countless lives."
"It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected," she said. "I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."
Prosecutors and jurors in Pike's initial criminal case, as well as the judges who presided over that trial and her numerous appeals, have often described Slemmer's murder as brutal and horrific. Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, told the Knoxville News-Sentinel after Pike's conviction in 1996 that she believed Pike was "evil," and the state "should kill her right away."
Records from Pike's trial show that Slemmer was repeatedly beaten and cut with both a meat cleaver and box cutter over the course of 30 minutes or an hour, in a wooded section of the University of Tennessee's campus.
When her body was found, a piece of the skull was missing and pentagrams had been carved into her forehead and chest, details that fueled a media firestorm and coincided with the "Satanic Panic" that swept the country in the 80s and 90s. Fellow students said Pike later bragged about the killing, revealing to one that she had removed and kept the missing piece of Slemmer's skull as a "souvenir."
Pike's boyfriend at the time of the killing, Tadaryl Shipp, and her friend, Shadolla Peterson, both helped her carry out Slemmer's murder, according to court records. Because Shipp was 17 at the time, he wasn't eligible for the death penalty and, instead, received a lifetime prison sentence. His parole was denied last year, but the case will be up for review again toward the end of 2031. Peterson faced probation, exclusively, in the wake of the murder after testifying against Pike at her trial.
Although Pike confessed to the crime, her legal team has filed numerous appeals challenging her death sentence and questioning whether she would still receive it if her case were tried today.
When Pike received her sentence at 20, in 1996, she was the youngest woman sent to death row in the United States' modern era of capital punishment. Now, she would be the only U.S. inmate put to death since that era began who was 18, 19 or 20 when their crimes were committed, if Wednesday's execution goes ahead. It would also mark Tennessee's first execution of a woman since at least 1820, according to research on the death penalty in early America.
Her attorneys have said Pike's history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect, as well as psychological conditions including PTSD, bipolar disorder and congenital brain damage, were not adequately represented in her original trial. They have also highlighted that, had Pike been just months younger at the time of the murder, she would not have been eligible to face capital punishment in Tennessee.
"In sentencing Pike to death, we rule out the possibility that her crime was a product of the immature mind of youth rather than fixed depravity," wrote U.S. Circuit Judge Jane Stranch in a concurring opinion on one of Pike's unsuccessful appeals in 2018. Despite siding with the majority's rule against her, Stranch acknowledged the controversy around Pike's death sentence, writing that "we presume that she is incapable of reform even though the stories of other teenage killers, many of whom have been rehabilitated behind bars, reveal other possibilities."
Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, told CBS News last year that declining national support for capital punishment and the low rates of death sentences handed down to teenagers suggest Pike would have received a different sentence in contemporary times.
"Society's view of who is truly deserving of a death sentence has changed in the years since Christa Pike was sentenced," Maher said. "Her young age, mental illness, and the physical and mental abuse she suffered at the time of her crime would likely persuade a jury today she is not someone who should receive a death sentence."
Women rarely receive death sentences in the U.S. and make up just 1% of death row inmates nationwide. Of around 2,000 people currently set to be executed around the country, just 45 are women, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which publishes data on capital punishment but doesn't take a position on it. Seventeen of those women have been sentenced to death in California, which has a moratorium on executions and hasn't carried one out in more than 20 years.
Throughout most of Pike's time in prison, she wasn't allowed to interact with other people. Among the lawsuits that her attorneys have filed, alongside their appeals, was one in which they likened her incarceration to solitary confinement because she was the only woman on Tennessee's death row for all but three of the years she spent behind bars. Another woman, Gaile Owens, was held in the same facility as Pike for those three years before her death sentence was ultimately commuted, but the two never had contact, court filings show.
Arguing that decades of isolation violated Pike's constitutional rights, the lawsuit ended in a settlement with the state in 2024 that granted her more opportunities to interact with other inmates.
Pike was returned to solitary confinement as her execution date approached, as Tennessee's lethal injection protocol requires for 14 days prior to an execution, her lawyers said in their latest appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Christopher Reeve's son Will has revealed he was diagnosed with a rare form of testicular cancer earlier this year.
Will, 34, whose mother is the late Dana Reeve, said he was alerted to the disease after he noticed a tender lump on one of his testicles in the shower in April – and his wife Amanda, 30, urged him to get an ultrasound.
The Good Morning America presenter told People he was left 'stunned' by the diagnosis and initially thought 'it was nothing or would go away' - adding his treatment brought back painful memories of his mother's treatment for lung cancer and his father's health struggles after he became quadriplegic.
Will was days away from his third birthday when his Superman star father was left paralyzed from the neck down after being thrown from a horse during an equestrian competition in Culpeper, Virginia, in May 1995 aged 42.
He relied upon a wheelchair and ventilator for the rest of his life. Tragically Will was orphaned just 17 months after Reeve's death from heart failure when mom Dana died from lung canc er aged 44 in 2006.
In early May, Will underwent an orchiectomy to remove the cancerous testicle and did sperm banking to ensure the couple would be able to start a family one day.

While the couple hoped the diagnosis would be a 'momentary blip' they learned 95 per cent of the cancer found was embryonal carcinoma, a rare and aggressive form of the disease which typically affects young men aged 15-35.
Will underwent a six hour surgery on June 10 to remove 'some dozens' of lymph nodes in his abdomen – three of which tested positive for testicular cancer.
The Good Morning America presenter then had two rounds of chemotherapy  - 20 years after his mother's cancer battle.
Will said, 'The irony is not lost on me that 20 years after my mom died of lung cancer at Memorial Sloan Kettering, there I was in the same building getting treated for cancer.
'I was experiencing life as each of my parents at the same time. Because I was a cancer patient at Memorial Sloan Kettering, I was getting a firsthand experience at what my mother went through.
'Simultaneously, I was learning more about what it was like to be my dad in the final nine years of his life, where he had my mom and our family taking care of him.
'I’ve had a lot happen in my life. But none of it until now had happened to me in a way.

'My dad got injured and then the next nine years a lot of our focus was taking care of him and making sure that we had as full and happy a life as possible, while also facing the realities of my dad being paralyzed and in a wheelchair, unable to move or breathe on his own.
'And then he died, and I had to learn what grief was. And shortly after that, my mom, who had never smoked, gets sick with lung cancer and then dies, and I learned grief all over again at a different level.'
Will underwent chemotherapy straight from work at GMA and likened the side effects of the treatment, including bone pain, to an 'ailment whack-a-mole.'
His second round of chemotherapy ended on July 31.
Will is now cancer-free, as of a check-up on September 8, and will have scans and bloodwork three to four times a year to check for any recurrence of the disease.
The five-year survival rate for embryonal carcinoma is over 98 per cent for early-stage disease and ranges from 74 per cent to 80 per cent for advanced, widespread disease, per The Cleveland Clinic.
As well as Amanda, Will credits the support of his family and friends, especially siblings Matthew, 46, and Alexandra, 42, for getting him through.
After the loss of his parents, Will was raised by the family's next door neighbors and close friends.

articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Homeland Security Money Financed Pro-Trump Television Ads
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump’s administration paid for TV ads showing him in a favorable light using money intended for U.S. Customs and Border Protection, an official and a top Republican senator confirmed to NBC News.
The source of the funding for the controversial ads the White House has described as public service announcements was first reported by The Wall Street Journal .
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees CBP, referred requests for comment to the White House, which did not immediately respond.
The unusual ads — one of which is nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad — include disclaimers stating they were paid for by the U.S. government. The administration’s apparent use of taxpayer money to produce ads that resemble campaign advertisements has drawn bipartisan criticism.
“It’s a great message. I like the message,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Monday of the most recent ad, “but it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said Monday only Trump would have “the audacity to force Americans not only to watch his propaganda, but to pay for it.”
Speaking to reporters Tuesday, Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, confirmed the official’s account of the source of the funds, saying that “it was taken out of funding that was supposed to be for Customs and Border Protection” in Trump’s so-called big, beautiful bill , which Republicans passed along party lines in 2025.
Collins, who faces a difficult re-election bid this fall, said the Appropriations Committee she chairs had no role in the money that the White House used. In fact, she said appropriations bills to fund the government typically have restrictions against using one account for another purpose.
“That’s why the administration went around the appropriations process and used an account that was part of the reconciliation bill,” Collins said in the Capitol.
The first of the ads aired earlier this month and featured Trump describing how he wanted to “defeat communism,” set to the song “Love Me” by JMSN . (Lawyers for JMSN on Monday sent a cease-and-desist letter to the White House telling it to stop using his music.)
The second spot closely tracks a 2024 Trump presidential campaign ad. It shows Trump walking down a hallway as he asks people in a voiceover to join him in his “final battle” to “demolish the deep state” and “expel the warmongers from our government.”
The political ad-tracking firm AdImpact has estimated that the administration has spent more than $1.7 million to run the ads.
Earlier in Trump’s term, DHS used taxpayer money to run a series of ads featuring then-Secretary Kristi Noem encouraging immigrants living in the United States illegally to self-deport.
Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., who provided a key vote to pass the megabill, cast doubt on the wisdom of Trump’s decision when asked if pulling the money from CBP was a good move.
“Well, if that’s exactly what happened, probably not,” Justice said, while adding that he’s not an expert on the legality of the move. “But at the same time, I don’t know the particulars to say, well, that those dollars can be used that way, or they can’t be used that way. I don’t know. I just don’t know.”
“I can’t imagine how smart the people in the administration are that they’ve done something that’s just going to fly right in their face,” Justice said. “I can’t imagine that they’ve done something that they know is not right, not ethical, not whatever. I just couldn’t imagine they’d do that. They’re too smart for that.”
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who announced his retirement last year after clashing with Trump on the megabill, tore into the president’s decision to fund those ads with taxpayer money.
“I hate it. I tell you, it feels like Viktor Orbán talking to the Hungarian people. There’s no place for that sort of thing,” Tillis said, while adding that Trump could have used political resources if he wanted to run a political ad. “If it were, you know, some clear message that was going to appeal to the broader, a real public service announcement, that’s fine. But that was not that.”
I am NBC News’ Senior Homeland Security Correspondent.

AI giant Anthropic has warned that its technology poses ‘existential risks to humanity’ as it gears up for one of the most highly valued stock market flotations in history.
In an unusual move, the start-up company behind the Claude tool highlighted the risks associated with its models – which it says could manipulate, blackmail and exhibit other ‘self-preserving behaviours’.
The California-based firm is hoping to achieve a valuation of $2trillion (£1.5trillion) when it goes on the market later this year.
Anthropic has dedicated almost a third of its 261-page prospectus to laying out the risk factors, nearly twice the 48 pages it has used to describe its business.
The formal warning to potential investors comes just two weeks after senior AI bosses, including Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei, called for a slowdown in the breakneck development of the technology – a warning echoed by rivals.
'Our development of highly advanced models, platforms and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm,' Anthropic said in the IPO prospectus.
The filing reveals Anthropic is targeting a potential valuation of $2trillion, more than double its estimated $965billion value in May and eclipsing SpaceX's blockbuster $1.78trillion flotation in June.
Catastrophic: Anthropic warns of the risks advanced AI poses to humanity as it targets IPO
Like Elon Musk's firm, Anthropic is spending billions of dollars on technology. The prospectus shows the company spent $7.33billion on computing and infrastructure last year, three times more than 2024, and is forecasting $518billion over the coming year.
At the same time, Anthropic revealed operating losses exceeding $8billion, and warned that nearly a quarter of its revenue came from two clients and many of its largest customers could cut spending.
The IPO, which is expected after the US midterm elections in November, comes as concerns over AI have intensified and firms have revealed major breaches.
Anthropic last week released a new version of its Opus model, a week after Amodei called for the sector to pace development. He has previously warned that a swarm of AI agents may be able to take over the internet in six months to a year unless firms spend more time on developing safety protocols.
Anthropic has in recent weeks vowed to disclose more data publicly about how it uses its models to build future technology, as experts warn about 'recursive self improvement' – when models can develop on their own without external help.
'We believe building reliable, trustworthy, and secure AI systems is a collective responsibility and that the market will reward it,' Anthropic said in the filing.
Separately, OpenAI today announced plans to delay its new model over safety concerns as it comes under intense scrutiny.
The firm, led by Sam Altman, said the system 'didn't quite meet the bar' of its standards, just days after it was revealed its model had accessed Australian government websites and systems without authorisation.
It is not yet clear whether UK retail investors will be granted access to the Anthropic IPO, as they were with SpaceX.
The SpaceX IPO was the first ever use of the Financial Conduct Authority's Public Offer Platform regime, which came into effect in January.
It allowed over 100,000 UK investors to buy shares in Elon Musk's firm, paving the way for other US firms, such as Anthropic, to follow suit.
Once Anthropic has set a date for its IPO, trading platforms in the UK will have a clearer idea of whether there is an allocation for DIY investors.
If not, investors will need to wait until the first day of its listing, when the shares should become freely tradeable.
